652.title: Yom Kippur: ask first
652.hook: before the day, people ask one another's forgiveness
652.howItsDone: In the days before Yom Kippur, especially on its eve, many Jews ask family, friends and coworkers for forgiveness (mechilah), and many say a prayer before Kol Nidre declaring that they forgive anyone who wronged them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shabbat Shuvah and Hosea's call. Your line was return. Today, the one thing Yom Kippur can't do by itself.

The afternoon before Yom Kippur has its own sounds. Phones buzzing with messages: if I hurt you this year, I'm sorry. Neighbors stopping each other on the street. A teenager, mortified, knocking on a sister's bedroom door. Some of it is a little formal, a habit. Some of it is the hardest conversation of the year. People do this because of one line in the Mishnah, and once you hear it, the whole holiday looks different.
screen: `PHONES BUZZING: I'M SORRY.` → `A KNOCK ON A SISTER'S DOOR.` → `ONE LINE IN THE MISHNAH.`

segments.voice: The line is at the very end of tractate Yoma, the Mishnah's book about Yom Kippur. Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah teaches: for wrongs between a person and God, Yom Kippur atones. For wrongs between a person and another person, Yom Kippur does not atone, until you have appeased the other person. A whole day of fasting and prayer, the day the Torah sets aside for atonement, cannot fix what you did to your neighbor. Only your neighbor can. So you go first. You ask. The Talmud and later law work out the details. Later authorities say to name what you did, not stay vague. If the person refuses, you try again, up to three times, bringing a few friends along to help make peace. If they still refuse after that, the burden lifts from you. There's a rule for the other side, too. Maimonides writes that a person shouldn't be cruel and refuse to forgive: when someone sincerely asks, forgive with a whole heart and a willing spirit. Not every hurt can be fixed in an afternoon. Teachers are careful to say that forgiveness isn't the same as trust, and that no one is required to put themselves back in danger. But the shape is clear. Before you stand before God asking to be forgiven, stand in front of the people you hurt. Then the day can do its work. The Hebrew word for this kind of forgiveness is mechilah, which some teachers explain as letting go of a debt.
screen: `BETWEEN YOU AND GOD.` · `BETWEEN YOU AND YOUR NEIGHBOR.` · `UP TO THREE TIMES.` · `DON'T BE CRUEL; FORGIVE.` · then, large: `ASK BEFORE THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Go past the obvious one and look for the hurt you filed as too small or too old to mention, a joke at someone's expense, a promise that quietly lapsed, a message never answered, and name the specific thing, the way the later authorities ask. Then turn it around, as Maimonides does: is someone trying to ask you, and have you made it hard for them? If you pray, you can ask God for an open hand in both directions.
Yom Kippur. The day of atonement, which, the Mishnah says, can't atone for wrongs between people until they make peace.
Your line: ask before the day. Between people, it's the people who have to come first. Until tomorrow.

653.title: Yom Kippur: releasing vows
653.hook: the evening begins by annulling rash vows, sung three times
653.howItsDone: Kol Nidre is chanted at the start of Yom Kippur evening, before sunset, with Torah scrolls held beside the cantor; it is repeated three times and followed by the verse from Numbers 15:26.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mishnah's rule: wrongs between people need the people first. Your line was ask before the day. Today, the first words of Yom Kippur itself.

The sun is still up. The synagogue is full, many dressed in white. The ark opens, and Torah scrolls are carried out and held on either side of the prayer leader, like witnesses. The room goes quiet. Then the cantor begins a melody so famous that composers have written concert pieces on it. The words aren't a prayer at all. They're a legal formula, in Aramaic, sung three times, each a little louder.
screen: `THE SUN IS STILL UP.` → `SCROLLS HELD LIKE WITNESSES.` → `A LEGAL FORMULA, SUNG.`

segments.voice: Kol Nidre means all vows. The text declares that all vows, oaths and promises we make to God, and fail to keep, are released, void, not binding. Why open Yom Kippur with that? The Torah takes vows seriously: "When a man voweth a vow unto the LORD, or sweareth an oath to bind his soul with a bond, he shall not break his word." People make rash promises to God in a moment of fear or anger: if I get through this, I'll never, I'll always. Then they can't keep them. Kol Nidre clears those words before standing in judgment. Before it begins, a line gives permission to pray together with sinners, with everyone, whatever their past. Right after comes a verse from Numbers: the whole community shall be forgiven, "and the stranger that sojourneth among them." Some important limits. Kol Nidre covers only personal vows between a person and God. It has never released promises made to other people, contracts or oaths in court. Medieval rabbis argued about it, and some great authorities wanted it removed. In later centuries, enemies of the Jews twisted it into a false charge that a Jew's word couldn't be trusted, which it never meant. Rabbeinu Tam championed a change in the wording, to look forward: vows from this Yom Kippur to the next. Many Ashkenazi communities say it that way. Its staying power may be the melody, and the honesty. Who in that room has never said something to heaven and then not kept it?
screen: `KOL NIDRE: ALL VOWS.` · `RASH PROMISES TO GOD.` · `NEVER PROMISES TO PEOPLE.` · `FROM THIS YOM KIPPUR TO THE NEXT.` · then, large: `RELEASE THE VOWS.`

segments.voice: Think of something you vowed to yourself, or to heaven, in a hard moment, that you haven't kept and maybe never could, like I'll never eat sugar again or I'll call every day, and name it honestly. Then set it down with relief, not guilt: if you pray, bring it to God and ask to be released; if not, simply say, I set this down. Then ask whether a smaller, real promise belongs in its place.
Kol Nidre. All vows. The Aramaic formula, sung three times at the start of Yom Kippur, releasing unkept personal vows to God.

654.title: Yom Kippur: white
654.hook: many wear white, like angels and like burial shrouds
654.tomorrow: Yom Kippur: the high priest's day
654.howItsDone: In many Ashkenazi communities men wear a white kittel on Yom Kippur (and some on Rosh Hashanah); women and Sephardi worshippers often dress in white; many avoid leather shoes on Yom Kippur as one of the day's afflictions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kol Nidre, all vows, sung three times before sunset. Your line was release the vows. Today, what people are wearing in that room.

Look around a traditional synagogue on Yom Kippur night and the colors are gone. Men in plain white robes over their clothes, tied with a simple belt. Women in white blouses and dresses. White covers on the ark and the reading table. Feet in canvas sneakers or socks, because many don't wear leather today. It looks a little like a wedding, and a little like a funeral. In a way, it's both.
screen: `THE COLORS ARE GONE.` → `PLAIN WHITE ROBES.` → `A WEDDING, AND A FUNERAL.`

segments.voice: The white robe is called a kittel, a Yiddish word for a smock: white cotton or linen, no pockets to speak of, often tied with a white belt. In many Ashkenazi communities, men wear it on Yom Kippur, and some on Rosh Hashanah too. And it shows up at the big doors of a life. Many grooms wear a kittel under the wedding canopy. Many leaders of the Passover seder wear one. And many are buried in one, or in plain white shrouds like it. Why white on Yom Kippur? The great sixteenth-century authority Rabbi Moshe Isserles gives two reasons, and they pull in opposite directions. First, white is the clothing of angels. On this day, without food or drink, people are said to be like angels, beyond the body's needs, praising all day long. Second, the kittel is like a burial shroud. Wearing it humbles the heart: it reminds you that life is short and that you'll stand before God with nothing but who you've been. Pure and mortal, angelic and dust, at once. Behind both is a verse from Isaiah, quoted all through these days: "though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow." Sephardi communities don't usually wear the kittel itself, but many dress in white, and white clothing is a widespread custom, not a rule for everyone. The point isn't fashion. When everyone wears the same plain white, the rich and the poor look alike. You stand there as a person, nothing more.
screen: `KITTEL: A WHITE SMOCK.` · `WEDDING, SEDER, BURIAL.` · `LIKE ANGELS.` · `LIKE A SHROUD.` · then, large: `DRESSED IN WHITE.`

segments.voice: If you can, change into something plain, no logos, no jewelry, nothing that tells the world who you are, or just take off one thing, a watch or a ring, and notice what's left when the signals are gone. If you pray, picture standing before God dressed like everyone else; if not, picture standing in a room where nobody can tell who's important.
Kittel. The plain white robe worn on Yom Kippur, at weddings and at the seder, like an angel's garment and like a shroud.
Your line: dressed in white. Like angels, and like a shroud, both at once. See you tomorrow.

655.title: Yom Kippur: the high priest's day
655.hook: the service retells the high priest entering the holy of holies
655.howItsDone: During the Musaf service of Yom Kippur, the prayer leader chants the Avodah, a poetic account of the high priest's service, and in many Ashkenazi congregations worshippers kneel and bow fully to the floor when the high priest's confession is recalled.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the kittel, white like angels and like shrouds. Your line was dressed in white. Today, another man in white, long ago.

Late on Yom Kippur morning, something unusual happens in many synagogues. The prayer leader begins to tell a story. Not pray it: tell it, step by step, like a narrator. At certain lines, the whole congregation does something seen only in these Days of Awe: they get down on their knees and bow their foreheads to the floor. The story is about one man, in one room, on one day of the year, in a Temple that no longer stands.
screen: `THE LEADER TELLS A STORY.` → `FOREHEADS TO THE FLOOR.` → `ONE MAN, ONE ROOM, ONE DAY.`

segments.voice: This is the Avodah, the service: a poetic retelling of the high priest's work on Yom Kippur, based on Leviticus sixteen and the Mishnah's tractate Yoma. The Torah's rule was strict. The high priest could enter the innermost room of the sanctuary, the holy of holies, only on this day, once in the year. The day was long and exacting. The Mishnah says he immersed his body five times, moving between golden garments and simple white linen, which he wore for the holiest parts. He confessed three times: for himself and his household, then for the priests, then for all Israel. In those confessions he spoke God's four-letter name aloud, the Name itself. The Mishnah says that when the people in the courtyard heard it, they knelt, bowed, fell on their faces, and called out: blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom for ever and ever. That's the moment congregations reenact on the floor today. Then he went in alone, carrying burning coals and incense, into a small dark room. And the Mishnah preserves a detail: coming out, he said only a short prayer in the outer room, and didn't linger, so as not to frighten the people waiting outside. Everyone was holding their breath. The Torah gives the purpose: "For on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins shall ye be clean before the LORD." When he came out safely, the Mishnah adds, he made a feast for his friends. With no Temple today, words take the place of the service, and once a year the whole room tells the story.
screen: `AVODAH: THE SERVICE.` · `WHITE LINEN, FIVE IMMERSIONS.` · `THE NAME, AND FACES ON THE FLOOR.` · `A SHORT PRAYER COMING OUT.` · then, large: `ONCE A YEAR.`

segments.voice: Go back to a moment in your life that felt set apart, a birth, a death, a vow, a silence under a huge sky, something that happened once and couldn't be repeated: where were you standing, what did the air feel like, who was waiting outside? If you pray, you can thank God for it; if not, let it be holy again for a minute, without explaining it.
Avodah. Service. The Yom Kippur retelling of the high priest's day, when congregations bow to the floor at the sound of the Name.

656.title: Yom Kippur: Jonah
656.hook: the afternoon reads Jonah, and the whole city of Nineveh turns
656.howItsDone: At the afternoon (Mincha) service of Yom Kippur, the entire book of Jonah is chanted as the haftarah, followed by verses from Micah in many communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Avodah, the high priest's day. Your line was once a year. Today, the late afternoon of Yom Kippur, when people are hungry and tired, and someone reads a story about a fish.

It's three or four in the afternoon. The fast is nearly a day old. Heads ache. Somebody's dozing in the back row. And at the afternoon service, the reader chants the whole book of Jonah: four short chapters. A prophet runs away from God, gets thrown off a ship in a storm, spends three days inside a great fish, and finally goes where he was sent. The fish is what sticks. But the reason to read it today comes after the fish.
screen: `THREE IN THE AFTERNOON, FASTING.` → `A PROPHET RUNS.` → `AFTER THE FISH.`

segments.voice: Jonah is sent to Nineveh, that great city, the capital of Israel's enemy. He runs. Later he says why: he knew God was gracious and would relent, and he didn't want the city spared. When he finally arrives, his whole sermon is five Hebrew words: yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown. And then, astonishingly, it works. The people of Nineveh believe. They fast. Everyone puts on sackcloth, from the greatest to the least. The king gets up from his throne, sits in ashes, and orders even the animals to fast. Then the line: "And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, which He said He would do unto them; and He did it not." The Mishnah, in tractate Taanit, points out what that verse doesn't say. It doesn't say God saw their sackcloth and their fasting. It says God saw their works: their deeds changed. That's a sharp message for a room full of people fasting right now. The fast alone, the Mishnah suggests, isn't what's seen; what changes afterward is. The book ends with Jonah angry outside the city, and God asking him about mercy: should I not have pity on Nineveh, that great city, with more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who can't tell their right hand from their left, "and also much cattle?" The book ends on that question, without Jonah's answer. If even Nineveh can turn, the reasoning goes, so can anyone in this room.

segments.voice: Think of someone you've written off, not someone dangerous, just someone you've decided is like that and always will be, and picture them a year from now, having changed one thing. If you pray, you can pray for their turning and for your own patience; if not, simply leave the door open a crack.
Yom Kippur. The day of atonement, whose afternoon reading is Jonah, and a whole enemy city that turned.

657.title: Yom Kippur: one long blast
657.hook: Neilah ends with a single long shofar note and "next year in Jerusalem"
657.howItsDone: The Neilah service closes Yom Kippur with the ark open throughout; it ends with the Shema, 'Baruch shem' three times, 'The LORD, He is God' seven times, a single long shofar blast and 'next year in Jerusalem.'

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jonah and the city that turned. Your line was even Nineveh. Today, the last hour of Yom Kippur.

The sun is going down. Nearly a full day without food or water. People who've been sitting stand up, because the ark has been opened, and it will stay open for the whole last service. Many stand for all of it. Legs ache. Voices are hoarse. Some who went home at midday are back, and the room fills up again for this hour. The service has a name that sounds like a door swinging shut.
screen: `THE SUN GOING DOWN.` → `THE ARK STAYS OPEN.` → `A DOOR SWINGING SHUT.`

segments.voice: It's called Neilah, the closing, or the locking. The ancient sources debate what's being closed. One view: the gates of the Temple, locked at the end of the day. Another: the gates of heaven, closing as the day ends. Either way, the image is a gate, still open, just barely. The words change. All through the ten days, the prayers asked: write us in the book of life. Now, in Neilah, they ask: seal us. Chotmenu. Write becomes seal. The service builds, and at the very end comes a sequence everyone knows. The congregation says the Shema's first line once. Then blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom, three times, out loud, the line usually whispered. Then a verse from Elijah's contest on Mount Carmel, when the people saw fire fall from heaven and cried out: "The LORD, He is God; the LORD, He is God." It's said seven times, louder each time. And then the shofar. Not the long sets of Rosh Hashanah: one single, long blast, a tekiah gedolah, held as long as the blower's breath will last. Everyone answers together: l'shanah haba'ah b'Yerushalayim. Next year in Jerusalem. It's an odd way to end. Not we did it, or we're forgiven, but hope pointed forward: a long sound that doesn't break, and a promise about next year. Then people go home and eat.

658.title: From fasting to building
658.hook: many hammer the first nail of the sukkah as Yom Kippur ends
658.howItsDone: Many Jews begin building their sukkah on the night Yom Kippur ends, even if only by hammering one nail or setting up one pole, then finish it in the days before Sukkot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Neilah, the closing gate. Your line was one long blast. Today, what happens right after that blast.

Yom Kippur is over. Stars are out. People pour out of the synagogue, dizzy with hunger, heading for bagels and orange juice. And in some backyards, before anyone has sat down to eat, there's a strange sound: tap, tap, tap. Someone is out in the dark with a hammer and a flashlight, banging in a single nail, or setting up one pole. Then they go inside and eat. They've started building a hut.
screen: `STARS OUT, FAST OVER.` → `TAP, TAP, TAP.` → `ONE NAIL, THEN DINNER.`

segments.voice: The hut is a sukkah, the temporary booth for the festival of Sukkot. Leviticus sets Yom Kippur on the tenth of the month and Sukkot on the fifteenth: five days apart. The Torah says: "Ye shall dwell in booths seven days." Rabbi Moshe Isserles, the great Ashkenazi authority, records the custom: right after Yom Kippur, begin building the sukkah, so as to go from one mitzvah to the next. Some just hammer one nail that night, a token; others put up the whole frame. The idea behind it is old. A psalm says of the faithful: "They go from strength to strength." Later teachers read it as a rule of life. Don't leave a gap after something holy. When you finish one good thing, start the next while the energy is still warm. And look at the contrast. For ten days the focus was inward: judgment, books, confession, a day without food. Now the very next act is outward and physical: wood, nails, branches, a roof you can see the stars through. The year doesn't stay in the synagogue. The calendar itself moves the mood from awe to joy, from fasting to building. Some readers add a gentle reason: just after Yom Kippur, a person is as clean as they'll ever be, and the first thing they do is start a home. Not a palace. A hut with branches for a roof, begun with one nail, in the dark.
screen: `DWELL IN BOOTHS SEVEN DAYS.` · `FROM ONE MITZVAH TO THE NEXT.` · `FROM STRENGTH TO STRENGTH.` · `FROM INWARD TO OUTWARD.` · then, large: `FROM FASTING TO BUILDING.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've just finished, or will finish today, a task, a meal, a piece of work, even this lesson, and before the glow fades, choose the very first step of the next good thing and make it tiny: one nail. If you pray, you can ask for strength to go from strength to strength.
Sukkah. The booth: the temporary hut for the festival of Sukkot, whose building begins the moment Yom Kippur ends.
Your line: go from strength to strength. A week of ask before the day, release the vows, dressed in white, once a year, even Nineveh, one long blast. Until tomorrow.
